standing_assumptions: Setting. The work is a textbook: Aronow and Miller, Foundations of Agnostic Statistics (Cambridge University Press, 2019). Every statement is about random variables on a probability space; Part II adds i.i.d. sampling; Part III adds the missing-data and potential-outcomes models. Locations give the printed page and the one-based page of main.pdf (316 pp.; in the body, PDF page = printed page + 18). Statements were transcribed from the page images (the 110 dpi staged renders, with higher-resolution renders of the same PDF pages where subscripts were small) and compared with the text layer for wording. (S1) Probability space. [Definition 1.1.1, p. 6 (PDF p. 24)] A set $S$ of subsets of $\Omega$ is an event space if it satisfies the following: Nonempty: $S \ne \emptyset$. Closed under complements: if $A \in S$, then $A^C \in S$. Closed under countable unions: if $A_1, A_2, A_3, ... \in S$, then $A_1 \cup A_2 \cup A_3 \cup ... \in S$. [Definition 1.1.2, p. 7 (PDF p. 25)] Kolmogorov Axioms. Let $\Omega$ be a sample space, $S$ be an event space, and $P$ be a probability measure. Then $(\Omega, S, P)$ is a probability space if it satisfies the following: Non-negativity: $\forall A \in S$, $P(A) \ge 0$, where $P(A)$ is finite and real. Unitarity: $P(\Omega) = 1$. Countable additivity: if $A_1, A_2, A_3, ... \in S$ are pairwise disjoint, then $P(A_1 \cup A_2 \cup A_3 \cup ...) = P(A_1) + P(A_2) + P(A_3) + ... = \sum_i P(A_i)$. [Footnote 11, p. 8 (PDF p. 26)] This assumption [that $(\Omega, S, P)$ is a probability space] shall henceforth be implicit in all definitions and theorems referring to $\Omega$, $S$, and/or $P$. (S2) Random variables and their distributions. [Definition 1.2.1, p. 16 (PDF p. 34)] A random variable is a function $X : \Omega \to \mathbb{R}$ such that, $\forall r \in \mathbb{R}$, $\{\omega \in \Omega : X(\omega) \le r\} \in S$. [Definition 1.2.2, p. 16] Let $g : U \to \mathbb{R}$ be a function, where $X(\Omega) \subseteq U \subseteq \mathbb{R}$. Then, if $g \circ X : \Omega \to \mathbb{R}$ is a random variable, we say that $g$ is a function of $X$, and write $g(X)$ to denote the random variable $g \circ X$. [p. 17 (PDF p. 35)] we use $\Pr[\cdot]$ to denote the probability that some condition(s) on a random variable will hold, or, equivalently, the probability that the event defined by those conditions will occur. [Definition 1.2.4, p. 18 (PDF p. 36)] A random variable $X$ is discrete if its range, $X(\Omega)$, is a countable set. [Definition 1.2.5, p. 18] For a discrete random variable $X$, the probability mass function of $X$ is $f(x) = \Pr[X = x]$, $\forall x \in \mathbb{R}$. [Definition 1.2.11, p. 21 (PDF p. 39)] For a random variable $X$, the cumulative distribution function of $X$ is $F(x) = \Pr[X \le x]$, $\forall x \in \mathbb{R}$. [Definition 1.2.14, p. 24 (PDF p. 42)] A random variable $X$ is continuous if there exists a non-negative function $f : \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$ such that the CDF of $X$ is $F(x) = \Pr[X \le x] = \int_{-\infty}^{x} f(u)du$, $\forall x \in \mathbb{R}$. The function $f$ is called the probability density function (PDF). [Definition 1.2.15, p. 25 (PDF p. 43), as printed; see finding P001-C01-E002] For a continuous random variable $X$ with CDF $F$, the probability density function of $X$ is $f(x) = \left.\frac{dF(u)}{du}\right|_{u=x}$, $\forall x \in \mathbb{R}$. [Definition 1.2.20, p. 31 (PDF p. 49)] For a random variable $X$ with PMF/PDF $f$, the support of $X$ is $\mathrm{Supp}[X] = \{x \in \mathbb{R} : f(x) > 0\}$. [Definition 1.3.1, p. 31] Let $X$ and $Y$ be random variables. Then $X = Y$ if, $\forall\omega \in \Omega$, $X(\omega) = Y(\omega)$. [Definition 1.3.16, p. 38 (PDF p. 56)] Let $X$ and $Y$ be either two discrete random variables with joint PMF $f$ or two jointly continuous random variables with joint PDF $f$. Then $X$ and $Y$ are independent if, $\forall x, y \in \mathbb{R}$, $f(x, y) = f_X(x)f_Y(y)$. We write $X \perp\!\!\!\perp Y$. [Definition 1.4.1, p. 39 (PDF p. 57)] A random vector (of length $K$) is a function $\mathbf{X} : \Omega \to \mathbb{R}^K$ such that, $\forall\omega \in \Omega$, $\mathbf{X}(\omega) = (X_{[1]}(\omega), X_{[2]}(\omega), ..., X_{[K]}(\omega))$, where $\forall k \in \{1, 2, ..., K\}$, $X_{[k]}$ is a random variable. (S3) Expectations. [Definition 2.1.1, p. 45 (PDF p. 63)] For a discrete random variable $X$ with probability mass function (PMF) $f$, if $\sum_x |x|f(x) < \infty$, then the expected value of $X$ is $\mathrm{E}[X] = \sum_x xf(x)$. For a continuous random variable $X$ with probability density function (PDF) $f$, if $\int_{-\infty}^{\infty} |x|f(x)dx < \infty$, then the expected value of $X$ is $\mathrm{E}[X] = \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} xf(x)dx$. [Footnote 2, p. 45] This regularity condition (and the corresponding one in the continuous case) is known as absolute convergence. It is virtually always satisfied in practice, so we omit this technical condition from all subsequent discussion of expectations. [Footnote 3, p. 49 (PDF p. 67)] This theorem, and every subsequent theorem that we only prove for these two cases [two discrete random variables with joint PMF, or two jointly continuous random variables with joint PDF], also holds when one random variable is discrete and the other continuous. [Definition 2.1.12, p. 52 (PDF p. 70)] The variance of a random variable $X$ is $\mathrm{V}[X] = \mathrm{E}[(X - \mathrm{E}[X])^2]$. [Definition 2.1.15, p. 53 (PDF p. 71)] The standard deviation of a random variable $X$ is $\sigma[X] = \sqrt{\mathrm{V}[X]}$. [Definition 2.1.22, p. 57 (PDF p. 75)] For a random variable $X$ and $c \in \mathbb{R}$, the mean squared error of $X$ about $c$ is $\mathrm{E}[(X - c)^2]$. [Definition 2.2.1, p. 59 (PDF p. 77)] The covariance of two random variables $X$ and $Y$ is $\mathrm{Cov}[X, Y] = \mathrm{E}[(X - \mathrm{E}[X])(Y - \mathrm{E}[Y])]$. [Definition 2.2.5, p. 62 (PDF p. 80)] The correlation of two random variables $X$ and $Y$ with $\sigma[X] > 0$ and $\sigma[Y] > 0$ is $\rho[X, Y] = \frac{\mathrm{Cov}[X, Y]}{\sigma[X]\sigma[Y]}$. [Definition 2.2.10, p. 67 (PDF p. 85)] For discrete random variables $X$ and $Y$ with joint PMF $f$, the conditional expectation of $Y$ given $X = x$ is $\mathrm{E}[Y|X = x] = \sum_y yf_{Y|X}(y|x)$, $\forall x \in \mathrm{Supp}[X]$. For jointly continuous random variables $X$ and $Y$ with joint PDF $f$, the conditional expectation of $Y$ given $X = x$ is $\mathrm{E}[Y|X = x] = \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} yf_{Y|X}(y|x)dy$, $\forall x \in \mathrm{Supp}[X]$. [Definition 2.2.12, p. 68 (PDF p. 86)] For random variables $X$ and $Y$, the conditional variance of $Y$ given $X = x$ is $\mathrm{V}[Y|X = x] = \mathrm{E}[(Y - \mathrm{E}[Y|X = x])^2|X = x]$, $\forall x \in \mathrm{Supp}[X]$. [Definition 2.2.15, p. 69 (PDF p. 87)] For random variables $X$ and $Y$ with joint PMF/PDF $f$, the conditional expectation function of $Y$ given $X = x$ is $G_Y(x) = \mathrm{E}[Y|X = x]$, $\forall x \in \mathrm{Supp}[X]$. [p. 70 (PDF p. 88)] We write $\mathrm{E}[Y|X]$ to denote $G_Y(X)$; the conditional variance function is $H_Y(x) = \mathrm{V}[Y|X = x]$, and $\mathrm{V}[Y|X]$ denotes the random variable $H_Y(X)$. [Footnote 14, p. 70] Ignoring some unimportant measure-theoretic regularity conditions, namely $X(\Omega) = \mathrm{Supp}[X]$. The multivariate versions are Definitions 2.3.3 and 2.3.4 (p. 85, PDF p. 103) and the multivariate BLP, Definition 2.3.6 (p. 86, PDF p. 104; transcribed in the targets that use it). (S4) Sampling and asymptotics. [Definition 3.1.1, p. 92 (PDF p. 110)] Let $X_1, X_2, ..., X_n$ be random variables with CDFs $F_1, F_2, ..., F_n$, respectively. Let $F_A$ denote the joint CDF of the random variables with indices in the set $A$. Then $X_1, X_2, ..., X_n$ are independent and identically distributed if they satisfy the following: Mutually independent: $\forall A \subseteq \{1, 2, ..., n\}$, $\forall(x_1, x_2, ..., x_n) \in \mathbb{R}^n$, $F_A((x_i)_{i \in A}) = \prod_{i \in A} F_i(x_i)$. Identically distributed: $\forall i, j \in \{1, 2, ..., n\}$ and $\forall x \in \mathbb{R}$, $F_i(x) = F_j(x)$. [p. 92] When we have i.i.d. random variables $X_1, X_2, ..., X_n$, we use the unsubscripted letter $X$ to denote the random variable whose distribution the i.i.d. draws all share. So, for example, $\mathrm{E}[X]$ denotes the expected value common to $X_1, X_2, ..., X_n$, that is, $\mathrm{E}[X] = \mathrm{E}[X_1] = \mathrm{E}[X_2] = ... = \mathrm{E}[X_n]$. [Definition 3.2.1, p. 96 (PDF p. 114)] For i.i.d. random variables $X_1, X_2, ..., X_n$, a sample statistic is a function of $X_1, X_2, ..., X_n$: $T_{(n)} = h_{(n)}(X_1, X_2, ..., X_n)$, where $h_{(n)} : \mathbb{R}^n \to \mathbb{R}$, $\forall n \in \mathbb{N}$. [Definition 3.2.2, p. 97 (PDF p. 115)] For i.i.d. random variables $X_1, X_2, ..., X_n$, the sample mean is $\overline{X} = \frac{X_1 + X_2 + ... + X_n}{n} = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n} X_i$. [Definition 3.2.6, p. 99 (PDF p. 117)] Let $(T_{(1)}, T_{(2)}, T_{(3)}, ...)$ be a sequence of random variables and let $c \in \mathbb{R}$. Then $T_{(n)}$ converges in probability to $c$ if, $\forall\epsilon > 0$, $\lim_{n \to \infty}\Pr[|T_{(n)} - c| \ge \epsilon] = 0$, or equivalently, $\lim_{n \to \infty}\Pr[|T_{(n)} - c| < \epsilon] = 1$; written $T_{(n)} \xrightarrow{p} c$. [Definition 3.2.22, p. 108 (PDF p. 126)] Let $(T_{(1)}, T_{(2)}, T_{(3)}, ...)$ be a sequence of random variables with CDFs $(F_{(1)}, F_{(2)}, F_{(3)}, ...)$, and let $T$ be a random variable with CDF $F$. Then $T_{(n)}$ converges in distribution to $T$ if, $\forall t \in \mathbb{R}$ at which $F$ is continuous, $\lim_{n \to \infty} F_{(n)}(t) = F(t)$; written $T_{(n)} \xrightarrow{d} T$. [Definition 3.2.28, p. 112 (PDF p. 130)] An estimator $\hat\theta$ is asymptotically normal if $\sqrt{n}(\hat\theta - \theta) \xrightarrow{d} N(0, \phi^2)$, for some finite $\phi > 0$. [Definition 3.3.1, p. 116 (PDF p. 134)] For i.i.d. random variables $X_1, X_2, ..., X_n$, the empirical CDF $\hat F$ of $X$ is $\hat F(x) = \overline{\mathrm{I}(X \le x)}$, $\forall x \in \mathbb{R}$. [Definition 3.3.2, p. 118 (PDF p. 136)] A statistical functional is a function $T : \mathcal{F} \to \mathbb{R}$, where $\mathcal{F}$ is the set of all possible CDFs. [Definition 3.3.3, p. 118] For i.i.d. random variables $X_1, X_2, ..., X_n$ with common CDF $F$, the plug-in estimator of $\theta = T(F)$ is $\hat\theta = T(\hat F)$. The 'usual plug-in regularity conditions' (p. 120, PDF p. 138) are not formally defined in the book (footnote 31 names Hadamard differentiability with respect to the Kolmogorov distance and gives no formal definition). (S5) Regression. [Definition 4.1.2, pp. 146–147 (PDF pp. 164–165), with the plus sign before the last term supplied] For i.i.d. random vectors $(Y_1, \mathbf{X}_1), (Y_2, \mathbf{X}_2), ..., (Y_n, \mathbf{X}_n)$, the ordinary least squares (OLS) regression estimator is the function $\hat g(\mathbf{X}) = \hat\beta_0 + \hat\beta_1X_{[1]} + \hat\beta_2X_{[2]} + ... + \hat\beta_KX_{[K]}$ such that $\hat{\boldsymbol\beta} = (\hat\beta_0, \hat\beta_1, ..., \hat\beta_K) = \arg\min_{(b_0, b_1, ..., b_K) \in \mathbb{R}^{K+1}}\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\left(Y_i - (b_0 + b_1X_{[1]i} + b_2X_{[2]i} + ... + b_KX_{[K]i})\right)^2$. We refer to $\hat{\boldsymbol\beta}$ as the OLS coefficient estimator. [Definition 4.1.3, p. 148 (PDF p. 166)] the regressor matrix $\mathbb{X}$ is the $n \times (K + 1)$ matrix whose $i^{\mathrm{th}}$ row is $(1, X_{[1]i}, X_{[2]i}, \cdots, X_{[K]i})$. (S6) Parametric models. [Definition 5.1.1, pp. 178–179 (PDF pp. 196–197)] For a random variable $Y$ and random vector $\mathbf{X}$ of length $K$, a parametric model is a set of functions $g : \mathbb{R}^{K+1} \to \mathbb{R}$ indexed by a real-valued parameter vector $\boldsymbol\theta$ of length $\tau$: $\{g(y, \mathbf{x}; \boldsymbol\theta) : \boldsymbol\theta \in \boldsymbol\Theta\}$, where $\boldsymbol\Theta \subseteq \mathbb{R}^\tau$. The set $\boldsymbol\Theta$ is called the parameter space. The model is said to be true if $\exists\boldsymbol\theta \in \boldsymbol\Theta$ such that $f_{Y|\mathbf{X}}(y|\mathbf{x}) = g(y, \mathbf{x}; \boldsymbol\theta)$. [Definition 5.2.1, p. 186 (PDF p. 204)] the likelihood function is $\mathcal{L}(\mathbf{t}|Y, \mathbf{X}) = g(Y, \mathbf{X}; \mathbf{t})$, and for i.i.d. observations $\mathcal{L}(\mathbf{t}|\mathbf{Y}, \mathbb{X}) = \prod_{i=1}^{n}\mathcal{L}(\mathbf{t}|Y_i, \mathbf{X}_i)$. [Definition 5.2.2, pp. 186–187 (PDF pp. 204–205)] the maximum likelihood estimator of $\boldsymbol\theta$ is $\hat{\boldsymbol\theta}_{ML} = \arg\max_{\mathbf{t} \in \boldsymbol\Theta}\mathcal{L}(\mathbf{t}|\mathbf{Y}, \mathbb{X}) = \arg\max_{\mathbf{t} \in \boldsymbol\Theta}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\log\mathcal{L}(\mathbf{t}|Y_i, \mathbf{X}_i)$. (S7) Missing data. [Definition 6.1.1, pp. 208–209 (PDF pp. 226–227)] For an outcome variable $Y_i$, the stable outcomes model is $Y_i^* = -99$ if $R_i = 0$ and $Y_i$ if $R_i = 1$; that is, $Y_i^* = Y_iR_i + (-99)(1 - R_i)$, where $Y_i^*$ is the censored version of $Y_i$ and $R_i$ is an indicator for whether $Y_i$ is observed for unit $i$. [Footnote 2, p. 208] Since we are assuming i.i.d. sampling, our inferences do not depend on the unit subscript $i$. [Definition 6.1.5, p. 213 (PDF p. 231)] $Y_i$ is missing completely at random if $Y_i \perp\!\!\!\perp R_i$ and $\Pr[R_i = 1] > 0$. [Definition 6.1.8, p. 215 (PDF p. 233)] $Y_i$ is missing at random conditional on $\mathbf{X}_i$ if $Y_i \perp\!\!\!\perp R_i|\mathbf{X}_i$ and $\exists\epsilon > 0$ such that $\Pr[R_i = 1|\mathbf{X}_i] > \epsilon$. [Footnote 6, p. 215] For random variables $X$, $Y$, and $Z$ with joint PMF/PDF $f(x, y, z)$, $Y \perp\!\!\!\perp Z|X$ if, $\forall y, z \in \mathbb{R}$ and $\forall x \in \mathrm{Supp}[X]$, $f_{(Y,Z)|X}((y, z)|x) = f_{Y|X}(y|x)f_{Z|X}(z|x)$. [Definition 6.1.11, p. 217 (PDF p. 235)] the response propensity function is $p_R(\mathbf{x}) = \Pr[R_i = 1|\mathbf{X}_i = \mathbf{x}]$, $\forall\mathbf{x} \in \mathrm{Supp}[\mathbf{X}_i]$. (S8) Causal inference. [Definition 7.1.1, p. 236 (PDF p. 254)] For an outcome variable $Y_i$ and binary treatment variable $D_i$, the potential outcomes model is $Y_i = Y_i(1) \cdot D_i + Y_i(0) \cdot (1 - D_i)$, where $Y_i(0)$ denotes the potential outcome under control for unit $i$, and $Y_i(1)$ denotes the potential outcome under treatment for unit $i$. [Definition 7.1.2, p. 237 (PDF p. 255)] $\tau_i = Y_i(1) - Y_i(0)$. [Definition 7.1.3, p. 238 (PDF p. 256)] the average treatment effect (ATE) is $\mathrm{E}[\tau_i]$. [Definition 7.1.9, p. 244 (PDF p. 262)] $D_i$ is randomly assigned if $(Y_i(0), Y_i(1)) \perp\!\!\!\perp D_i$ and $0 < \Pr[D_i = 1] < 1$. [Definition 7.1.12, p. 247 (PDF p. 265)] $D_i$ is strongly ignorable conditional on $\mathbf{X}_i$ if $(Y_i(0), Y_i(1)) \perp\!\!\!\perp D_i|\mathbf{X}_i$ and $\exists\epsilon > 0$ such that $\epsilon < \Pr[D_i = 1|\mathbf{X}_i] < 1 - \epsilon$. [Definition 7.1.15, p. 250 (PDF p. 268)] the treatment propensity function is $p_D(\mathbf{x}) = \Pr[D_i = 1|\mathbf{X}_i = \mathbf{x}]$, $\forall\mathbf{x} \in \mathrm{Supp}[\mathbf{X}_i]$. Notes for the formalizer. (a) The book works with PMFs and PDFs and states pointwise conditions ('for all $x$'); for continuous variables these hold only up to null sets (finding P001-C01-E002), so a measure-theoretic formalization should read densities and conditional expectations as versions. (b) Existence and finiteness of the expectations in a statement is a standing convention (footnote 2, p. 45). (c) Asymptotic statements are about an infinite i.i.d. sequence and $n \to \infty$. (d) In a target's statement, text in square brackets is a label or a remark of the transcriber, not the book's words.

canonical_claim.name_in_paper: Section 3.3.1, the sentence 'our assumption about finite variance was sufficient to imply that the population mean is well behaved', read with footnote 31, as printed
canonical_claim.location: p. 120 (PDF p. 138), paragraph after Theorem 3.3.6, and footnote 31. The mean functional $T_{\mathrm{E}}$: p. 118 (PDF p. 136)
canonical_claim.statement: [Printed statement] We omit the proof, which requires empirical process theory. The conditions for $T$ to be well behaved at $F$ are often implied by other assumptions; for instance, our assumption about finite variance was sufficient to imply that the population mean is well behaved. We will refer to these assumptions, as they apply to the functional under consideration, as the usual plug-in regularity conditions. [Footnote 31, first two sentences] We say $T$ is well behaved if it is Hadamard differentiable at $F$ with respect to the Kolmogorov distance. Formally, the Kolmogorov distance between two distributions $F$ and $G$ is given by the value of the largest divergence between their two CDFs, $\sup_x |F(x) - G(x)|$. [What is refuted] That finite variance of $F$ implies Hadamard differentiability at $F$, with respect to the Kolmogorov distance, of the mean functional $T_{\mathrm{E}}(G) = \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} x dG(x)$, even when $T_{\mathrm{E}}$ is restricted to the CDFs with finite second moment. The CLT for the sample mean (Theorem 3.2.24) is not refuted. [Counterexample, from the validators (adjudicated)] Let $F$ be the CDF of the distribution with mass $q_k = 2^{-(k+1)}$ at each integer $k = 0, 1, 2, ...$. Then $\sum_k q_k = 1$, $\mathrm{E}_F[X] = 1$, $\mathrm{E}_F[X^2] = 3$ and $\mathrm{Var}_F[X] = 2$. For each integer $n \ge 2$ let $H_n$ be the CDF of $X + n$ for $X \sim F$, and let $G_n = (1 - n^{-3})F + n^{-3}H_n$ and $t_n = n^{-2}$. Then: (a) each $G_n$ is a CDF with the same support $\{0, 1, 2, ...\}$ as $F$ and finite second moment; $\mathrm{Var}_{G_n}[X]$ is finite and $\mathrm{Var}_{G_n}[X] \to 2$; (b) with $h_n = (G_n - F)/t_n$, $G_n = F + t_nh_n$ and $\|h_n\|_\infty = n^2 \cdot n^{-3}\sup_x |H_n(x) - F(x)| \le \frac{1}{n} \to 0$, so $h_n \to 0$ in sup norm and $t_n \to 0$; (c) $T_{\mathrm{E}}(G_n) - T_{\mathrm{E}}(F) = n^{-3}\left((1 + n) - 1\right) = n^{-2}$, so $\frac{T_{\mathrm{E}}(F + t_nh_n) - T_{\mathrm{E}}(F)}{t_n} = 1$ for every $n$. A Hadamard derivative at $F$ is a continuous linear map $L_F$, so it would require this quotient to converge to $L_F(0) = 0$. Hence $T_{\mathrm{E}}$ is not Hadamard differentiable at $F$ with respect to the Kolmogorov distance, although $F$ has finite variance.
canonical_claim.definitions_needed: In the standing assumptions: i.i.d. random variables and the convention that the unsubscripted $X$ denotes the common distribution (Definition 3.1.1 and p. 92); sample statistic $T_{(n)}$ (Definition 3.2.1); sample mean $\overline{X}$ (Definition 3.2.2); convergence in probability (Definition 3.2.6); convergence in distribution (Definition 3.2.22); asymptotic normality (Definition 3.2.28); empirical CDF $\hat F$ (Definition 3.3.1); statistical functional and plug-in estimator (Definitions 3.3.2, 3.3.3); and the definitions of Chapters 1 and 2 (expected value, variance, covariance, correlation). [p. 118] For the random variable $X$ with CDF $F$, we can write the expected value of $X$ as $\mathrm{E}[X] = T_{\mathrm{E}}(F) = \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} x dF(x)$. [Definition 3.3.2, p. 118] A statistical functional is a function $T : \mathcal{F} \to \mathbb{R}$, where $\mathcal{F}$ is the set of all possible CDFs. [Hadamard differentiability with respect to the sup distance, as used by the validators; the book gives no formal definition] there is a continuous linear map $L_F$ with $\frac{T(F + t_rh_r) - T(F)}{t_r} \to L_F(h)$ whenever $t_r \to 0$, $\|h_r - h\|_\infty \to 0$ and each $F + t_rh_r$ is a CDF in the domain.
canonical_claim.finite_lemmas: Exact for each $n$: $\sum_{k=0}^{K} q_k = 1 - 2^{-(K+1)}$, $\sum_{k=0}^{K} kq_k = 1 - (K + 2)2^{-(K+1)}$, $\sum_{k=0}^{K} k^2q_k = 3 - (K^2 + 4K + 6)2^{-(K+1)}$; for a mixture $G = (1 - p)F + pH_L$ with $H_L$ the law of $X + L$: $\mathrm{E}_G[X] = 1 + pL$ and $\mathrm{E}_G[X^2] = 3 + p(L^2 + 2L)$; $\sup_x |G(x) - F(x)| \le p$. With $p = n^{-3}$, $L = n$: $\mathrm{E}_{G_n}[X] - \mathrm{E}_F[X] = n^{-2}$ and $\mathrm{Var}_{G_n}[X] = 3 + n^{-3}(n^2 + 2n) - (1 + n^{-2})^2$.
canonical_claim.note: Error rated Moderate (dual validation, adjudicated; an external check of Wasserman 2006 is recorded in runs/P001/settle/settled.json). The witness is an exact rational family; the adjudicator's derivation restricts the functional to CDFs with finite second moment, the reading most favourable to the book. Under a weaker, non-continuous notion of derivative the sentence is not refuted by this sequence; the validators note that such a notion would not support Theorem 3.3.6.

canonical_claim.name_in_paper: Section 3.3.1, the example offered for the 'usual plug-in regularity conditions', corrected: asymptotic normality of the sample mean from the Central Limit Theorem, not from Hadamard differentiability of the mean
canonical_claim.location: p. 120 (PDF p. 138), paragraph after Theorem 3.3.6. Theorem 3.2.24: p. 109 (PDF p. 127). Example 3.3.4: p. 119 (PDF p. 137)
canonical_claim.statement: [Corrected passage] Replace 'for instance, our assumption about finite variance was sufficient to imply that the population mean is well behaved' by the scalar justification: for the population mean, the plug-in estimator is the sample mean (Example 3.3.4), and under finite variance $\mathrm{V}[X] > 0$ its asymptotic normality follows from the Central Limit Theorem (Theorem 3.2.24). When the functional delta method (Theorem 3.3.6) is invoked, suitable continuity, topology and tangent conditions must be specified. [Formal content] (i) For i.i.d. $X_1, X_2, ...$ with CDF $F$, finite $\mathrm{E}[X] = \mu$ and finite $\mathrm{V}[X] = \sigma^2 > 0$: $T_{\mathrm{E}}(\hat F) = \overline{X}$ and $\sqrt{n}(T_{\mathrm{E}}(\hat F) - T_{\mathrm{E}}(F)) \xrightarrow{d} N(0, \sigma^2)$, so the plug-in estimator of the mean is asymptotically normal in the sense of Definition 3.2.28 with $\phi = \sigma$. (ii) Finite variance of $F$ does not imply that $T_{\mathrm{E}}$ is Hadamard differentiable at $F$ with respect to the Kolmogorov distance: there is a CDF $F$ with finite variance and CDFs $G_n$ with finite variance such that $\sup_x |G_n(x) - F(x)|/t_n \to 0$ for a sequence $t_n \to 0$ while $(T_{\mathrm{E}}(G_n) - T_{\mathrm{E}}(F))/t_n = 1$ for all $n$ (the counterexample target for this finding).
canonical_claim.definitions_needed: In the standing assumptions: i.i.d. random variables and the convention that the unsubscripted $X$ denotes the common distribution (Definition 3.1.1 and p. 92); sample statistic $T_{(n)}$ (Definition 3.2.1); sample mean $\overline{X}$ (Definition 3.2.2); convergence in probability (Definition 3.2.6); convergence in distribution (Definition 3.2.22); asymptotic normality (Definition 3.2.28); empirical CDF $\hat F$ (Definition 3.3.1); statistical functional and plug-in estimator (Definitions 3.3.2, 3.3.3); and the definitions of Chapters 1 and 2 (expected value, variance, covariance, correlation). [Theorem 3.2.24, p. 109] Central Limit Theorem. Let $X_1, X_2, ..., X_n$ be i.i.d. random variables with (finite) $\mathrm{E}[X] = \mu$ and finite $\mathrm{V}[X] = \sigma^2 > 0$, and let $Z$ be the standardized sample mean. Then $Z \xrightarrow{d} N(0, 1)$, or equivalently, $\sqrt{n}(\overline{X} - \mu) \xrightarrow{d} N(0, \sigma^2)$. [p. 118] $T_{\mathrm{E}}(F) = \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} x dF(x)$. [Example 3.3.4, p. 119] the plug-in estimator of $\mathrm{E}[X]$ is $\hat{\mathrm{E}}[X] = T_{\mathrm{E}}(\hat F) = \overline{X}$.
canonical_claim.finite_lemmas: $T_{\mathrm{E}}(\hat F) = \int x d\hat F(x) = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n} X_i$ exactly, for each $n$ (Example 3.3.4, as corrected under P001-C03-E003); $\mathrm{E}[\overline{X}] = \mu$ and $\mathrm{V}[\overline{X}] = \sigma^2/n$ (Theorems 3.2.3, 3.2.4).
canonical_claim.note: Error rated Moderate: the one concrete case offered for the 'usual plug-in regularity conditions' does not satisfy them as footnote 31 defines them; the scalar CLT route is unaffected, and no reported number depends on the sentence. Part (i) is Theorem 3.2.24 restated for the plug-in estimator; part (ii) is the negative fact that replaces the printed claim.

canonical_claim.name_in_paper: Definition 4.3.7 (Partial Derivative at the Average) and the remark that the PDA 'has a well-defined meaning', as printed: a joint distribution for which the PDA is not determined
canonical_claim.location: Definition 4.3.7: p. 167 (PDF p. 185). Remark: p. 168 (PDF p. 186). Footnote 13: p. 166 (PDF p. 184). Definition 2.2.15: p. 69 (PDF p. 87)
canonical_claim.statement: [Printed statements] [p. 166] Let us assume that the CEF is differentiable with respect to a given variable $X_{[k]}$.$^{13}$ [Footnote 13] Beyond requiring that the CEF be differentiable at every value of $\mathbf{X}$ with positive support, this characterization only makes sense when $\mathbf{X}$ is continuous. [p. 167] Definition 4.3.7. Partial Derivative at the Average. For a random variable $Y$ and random vector $\mathbf{X}$, the partial derivative at the average of the CEF (of $Y$ given $\mathbf{X}$) with respect to $X_{[k]}$ is $PDA_{X_{[k]}} = \left.\frac{\partial\mathrm{E}[Y|\mathbf{X}]}{\partial X_{[k]}}\right|_{\mathbf{X} = \mathrm{E}[\mathbf{X}]}$. [p. 168] While the partial derivative at the average also has a well-defined meaning, it is limited to just one particular point on the probability distribution of the explanatory variables. [What is refuted] That $PDA_{X_{[k]}}$ is a well-defined feature of the joint distribution of $(Y, \mathbf{X})$ under the stated conditions (a CEF differentiable at every value of $\mathbf{X}$ with positive support, $\mathbf{X}$ continuous). The formula is not refuted where $\mathrm{E}[\mathbf{X}]$ is an interior point of the support. [Counterexample, from the validator] Let $X$ be a continuous random variable with PDF $f_X(x) = \frac{1}{2}$ for $x \in [-2, -1] \cup [1, 2]$ and 0 otherwise, and let $Y \sim U(-1, 1)$ be independent of $X$. Then: (a) $(X, Y)$ is jointly continuous and bounded; $\mathrm{E}[X] = 0$ and $0 \notin \mathrm{Supp}[X] = [-2, -1] \cup [1, 2]$; (b) the CEF, defined on $\mathrm{Supp}[X]$ (Definition 2.2.15), is $\mathrm{E}[Y|X = x] = 0$ for all $x \in \mathrm{Supp}[X]$, and is differentiable there; (c) the functions $m_0(x) = 0$ and $m_1(x) = x(1 - x^2)^2$ for $|x| < 1$, $m_1(x) = 0$ for $|x| \ge 1$, are both continuously differentiable on $\mathbb{R}$ and both equal the CEF at every $x \in \mathrm{Supp}[X]$; (d) $m_0'(0) = 0$ and $m_1'(0) = 1$; replacing $m_1$ by $a \cdot m_1$ gives derivative $a$ at 0 for any real $a$. So the derivative 'at the average' takes any real value depending on how the CEF is extended to the point $\mathrm{E}[X]$, with the joint distribution of $(Y, X)$ held fixed.
canonical_claim.definitions_needed: In the standing assumptions: i.i.d. random vectors $(Y_1, \mathbf{X}_1), ..., (Y_n, \mathbf{X}_n)$; the multivariate BLP (Definition 2.3.6); the CEF (Definition 2.2.15) and its domain $\mathrm{Supp}[\mathbf{X}]$; expected value, variance and covariance; convergence in probability (Definition 3.2.6); the OLS regression estimator (Definition 4.1.2) and the regressor matrix $\mathbb{X}$ (Definition 4.1.3). [Definition 2.2.15, p. 69] For random variables $X$ and $Y$ with joint PMF/PDF $f$, the conditional expectation function of $Y$ given $X = x$ is $G_Y(x) = \mathrm{E}[Y|X = x]$, $\forall x \in \mathrm{Supp}[X]$. [Definition 1.2.20, p. 31 (PDF p. 49)] $\mathrm{Supp}[X] = \{x \in \mathbb{R} : f(x) > 0\}$.
canonical_claim.note: Error rated Moderate: the definition omits the requirement that $\mathrm{E}[\mathbf{X}]$ be a point at which the CEF and its derivative are fixed by the distribution; the PDA rows of the application (Table 4.4.5) are read under it, but no number, example or theorem is shown wrong. A supplementary exact example of the validator (a square-frame support) shows that a connected joint support with full interval marginal supports does not suffice either.

canonical_claim.name_in_paper: Definition 4.3.7 (Partial Derivative at the Average), corrected with a support condition at the covariate mean
canonical_claim.location: p. 167 (PDF p. 185), Definition 4.3.7; p. 168 (PDF p. 186), first paragraph
canonical_claim.statement: [Corrected statement] Definition 4.3.7. Partial Derivative at the Average. For a random variable $Y$ and random vector $\mathbf{X}$ such that $\boldsymbol\mu = \mathrm{E}[\mathbf{X}]$ exists and there is an open neighborhood $U$ of $\boldsymbol\mu$ contained in the joint covariate support, with a continuous representative of the CEF on $U$ that is differentiable in coordinate $k$ at $\boldsymbol\mu$, the partial derivative at the average of the CEF (of $Y$ given $\mathbf{X}$) with respect to $X_{[k]}$ is $PDA_{X_{[k]}} = \left.\frac{\partial\mathrm{E}[Y|\mathbf{X}]}{\partial X_{[k]}}\right|_{\mathbf{X} = \mathrm{E}[\mathbf{X}]}$. [p. 168] Under this condition the partial derivative at the average has a well-defined meaning; without it, a derivative of a chosen predictor at $\mathrm{E}[\mathbf{X}]$ is an extrapolation-dependent summary of that predictor, not a feature of the CEF. [Formal content: the condition makes the PDA a functional of the joint distribution] Let $\mathbf{X}$ be a continuous random vector of length $K$ with PDF $f_{\mathbf{X}}$ and finite mean $\boldsymbol\mu$, let $U \subseteq \mathbb{R}^K$ be open with $\boldsymbol\mu \in U$ and $f_{\mathbf{X}}(\mathbf{x}) > 0$ for all $\mathbf{x} \in U$, and let $m, \tilde m : U \to \mathbb{R}$ be continuous functions with $m(\mathbf{x}) = \tilde m(\mathbf{x}) = \mathrm{E}[Y|\mathbf{X} = \mathbf{x}]$ for (Lebesgue-almost) every $\mathbf{x} \in U$. Then $m = \tilde m$ on $U$; in particular, if $m$ has a partial derivative with respect to $x_{[k]}$ at $\boldsymbol\mu$, so does $\tilde m$, and $\frac{\partial m}{\partial x_{[k]}}(\boldsymbol\mu) = \frac{\partial\tilde m}{\partial x_{[k]}}(\boldsymbol\mu)$. The condition is sufficient, not necessary.
canonical_claim.definitions_needed: In the standing assumptions: i.i.d. random vectors $(Y_1, \mathbf{X}_1), ..., (Y_n, \mathbf{X}_n)$; the multivariate BLP (Definition 2.3.6); the CEF (Definition 2.2.15) and its domain $\mathrm{Supp}[\mathbf{X}]$; expected value, variance and covariance; convergence in probability (Definition 3.2.6); the OLS regression estimator (Definition 4.1.2) and the regressor matrix $\mathbb{X}$ (Definition 4.1.3). [Definition 4.3.7 as printed, p. 167] $PDA_{X_{[k]}} = \left.\frac{\partial\mathrm{E}[Y|\mathbf{X}]}{\partial X_{[k]}}\right|_{\mathbf{X} = \mathrm{E}[\mathbf{X}]}$. [Footnote 13, p. 166] the CEF is required to be differentiable at every value of $\mathbf{X}$ with positive support, and $\mathbf{X}$ to be continuous. [Definition 1.2.20, p. 31 (PDF p. 49), read for a random vector as Section 1.4 indicates] $\mathrm{Supp}[\mathbf{X}] = \{\mathbf{x} \in \mathbb{R}^K : f_{\mathbf{X}}(\mathbf{x}) > 0\}$. [Definition 2.3.4, p. 85 (PDF p. 103)] For random variables $X_{[1]}, X_{[2]}, ..., X_{[K]}$, and $Y$ with joint PMF/PDF $f$, the CEF of $Y$ given $\mathbf{X} = \mathbf{x}$ is $G_Y(\mathbf{x}) = \mathrm{E}[Y|\mathbf{X} = \mathbf{x}]$, $\forall \mathbf{x} \in \mathrm{Supp}[\mathbf{X}]$.
canonical_claim.note: Error rated Moderate. The repair is a real support condition that the application is not shown to satisfy. The conditional expectation is determined by the distribution only up to null sets, which is why the formal statement speaks of a continuous representative; two continuous functions that agree almost everywhere on an open set agree on it. In Example 4.3.8 the mean $(\frac{1}{2}, \frac{1}{2})$ is interior to the support $(0, 1)^2$ and the CEF $-x_1$ is continuous near it, so the corrected definition gives the printed value $-1$.

canonical_claim.name_in_paper: Definition 4.3.9 (Polynomial Least Squares Sieve Estimator), the rate condition '$J_n \to \infty$ and $\frac{1}{n}J_n \to 0$' as a sufficient condition for consistency, as printed
canonical_claim.location: Section 4.3.5: p. 168 (PDF p. 186); Definition 4.3.9: pp. 168–169 (PDF pp. 186–187); the paragraph after it: p. 169 (PDF p. 187)
canonical_claim.statement: [Printed statements] [p. 168] As long as flexibility grows “slowly” enough relative to $n$, we can show that the estimator will be consistent. Definition 4.3.9. Polynomial Least Squares Sieve Estimator. For i.i.d. random vectors $(Y_1, X_1), (Y_2, X_2), ..., (Y_n, X_n)$, the polynomial least squares sieve estimator of the conditional expectation function is $\hat{\mathrm{E}}_n[Y|X = x] = \sum_{k=0}^{J_n}\hat\beta_kx^k$, [p. 169] where $\hat{\boldsymbol\beta} = \arg\min_{\mathbf{b} \in \mathbb{R}^{J_n+1}}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\left(Y_i - \sum_{k=0}^{J_n} b_kX_i^k\right)$, where $J_n \to \infty$ and $\frac{1}{n}J_n \to 0$. [p. 169] As $n \to \infty$, the degree of that polynomial $J_n \to \infty$, but at a slower rate. ... As long as the CEF is smooth with appropriate support across $X$, then $\hat{\mathrm{E}}[Y|X = x]$ will be consistent across regions of the data with nonzero probability mass (by the logic of Theorem 4.3.3, Polynomial Approximation of the CEF). [What is refuted] That, with the residual squared (the display's missing exponent is finding P001-C04-E003), the printed rate condition is sufficient for consistency of $\hat{\mathrm{E}}_n[Y|X = x]$ over regions of positive probability mass, for a smooth CEF with compact interval support. Consistency under a slower-growing degree is not refuted. [Counterexample, from the validators] Let $X \sim U(0, 1)$ and $Y \sim N(0, 1)$ be independent, so that the CEF is $m(x) = \mathrm{E}[Y|X = x] = 0$ on $[0, 1]$ (smooth; all moments exist). Let $\hat m_n$ be the least squares polynomial of degree $J_n = \lfloor n^{3/4} \rfloor$ fitted to $n$ i.i.d. draws. Then $J_n \to \infty$ and $J_n/n \to 0$, but for every fixed $\delta \in (0, 1]$ and every $\epsilon > 0$, $\liminf_{t \to \infty}\Pr\left[\int_0^\delta\hat m_{t^4}(x)^2dx > \epsilon\right] \ge \frac{1}{2}$ (limit over integers $t$, with $n = t^4$). So $\hat m_n$ does not converge to $m$ in probability in $L^2$ on $[0, \delta]$, a region of positive probability mass. A supplementary argument gives endpoint failure for a separate square-root-degree estimator sequence: for each integer $n \ge 1$, let $\tilde m_n$ be any polynomial of degree at most $\tilde J_n = \lfloor\sqrt n\rfloor$ that minimizes $\sum_{i=1}^n(Y_i-p(X_i))^2$ over all polynomials $p$ of degree at most $\tilde J_n$, where $(X_1, Y_1), \ldots, (X_n, Y_n)$ are i.i.d. draws of the same independent pair $X \sim U(0, 1)$, $Y \sim N(0, 1)$, and whose coefficients are Borel measurable functions of $(X_1, Y_1, \ldots, X_n, Y_n)$. For every such sequence and every integer $t \ge 2$ (so that $n = t^2$ and $\tilde J_{t^2} = t$), $\Pr\left[|\tilde m_{t^2}(1)| > \frac{1}{4}\right] \ge \frac{1}{4}$.
canonical_claim.definitions_needed: In the standing assumptions: i.i.d. random vectors $(Y_1, \mathbf{X}_1), ..., (Y_n, \mathbf{X}_n)$; the multivariate BLP (Definition 2.3.6); the CEF (Definition 2.2.15) and its domain $\mathrm{Supp}[\mathbf{X}]$; expected value, variance and covariance; convergence in probability (Definition 3.2.6); the OLS regression estimator (Definition 4.1.2) and the regressor matrix $\mathbb{X}$ (Definition 4.1.3). [Theorem 4.3.3, p. 158 (PDF p. 176)] Polynomial Approximation of the CEF. Let $X$ and $Y$ be random variables, and suppose that $\mathrm{E}[Y|X = x]$ is continuous and $\mathrm{Supp}[X] = [a, b]$. Then, $\forall \epsilon > 0$, $\exists K \in \mathbb{N}$ such that, $\forall K' \ge K$, $\mathrm{E}\left[\left(\mathrm{E}[Y|X] - g(X, X^2, ..., X^{K'})\right)^2\right] < \epsilon$, where $g(X, X^2, ..., X^{K'})$ is the BLP of $Y$ given $X, X^2, ..., X^{K'}$. [Reading of 'consistent across regions of the data with nonzero probability mass' used by the validators] for an interval $R$ with $\Pr[X \in R] > 0$, $\int_R(\hat m_n(x) - m(x))^2dx \xrightarrow{p} 0$.
canonical_claim.finite_lemmas: [Exact finite-sample steps of the validators' derivation] With $n$ distinct design points and degree $J < n$, conditional on $X_1, ..., X_n$ the fitted polynomial is linear in $(Y_1, ..., Y_n)$, so for any fixed linear functional $\ell$ of the fit (for example $\hat m_n(x_0)$, or a coefficient in an orthonormal basis of $L^2[0, \delta]$), $\ell(\hat m_n)$ is conditionally $N(0, v_n)$ with $v_n = \mathbf{a}^T(P^TP)^{-1}\mathbf{a}$ for the design matrix $P$ of the polynomial basis. A Chebyshev-polynomial construction gives $v_n \ge \frac{9t^4}{52428800}$ on a design event of probability at least $\frac{1}{2}$ for $n = t^4$; conditional Gaussianity then gives failure in probability. For the uniform design, with $p_k(x) = \sqrt{2k + 1}L_k(2x - 1)$ the orthonormal Legendre basis, $\mathrm{E}[p_j(X)p_k(X)] = \mathbb{1}\{j = k\}$ and $\sum_{k=0}^{J} p_k(x)^2 \le (J + 1)^2$.
canonical_claim.note: Error rated Moderate (dual validation; both validators confirmed with independent constructions). The counterexample does not contradict in-sample mean-square consistency, and does not establish failure at every interior point or a sharp threshold. The constant $\frac{9t^4}{52428800}$ and the probability bounds are from the validators' derivations (runs/P001/validate/P001-C04-E001/v1 and v2); they have not been re-derived here.
